title: Can a sealed class or interface be local or anonymous, and why not?
shortTitle: Can a sealed class/interface be local or anonymous — why not?

s1_definition.profdef: A sealed class or interface restricts which other classes or interfaces may extend or implement it, and the permitted subtypes must be known and nameable at compile time. A local class (declared inside a method) and an anonymous class (declared inline with `new SomeType() { ... }`) cannot be `sealed`, because sealing requires an explicit, stable set of permitted subtypes identified by name, and local or anonymous types have restricted or no names and restricted scope. The compiler therefore rejects the `sealed` modifier on local and anonymous classes.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India issuing a sealed rulebook that says "only these three named account products may extend AccountProduct: Savings, Current, and FixedDeposit." For that rule to mean anything, each permitted product must have an official, registered name that auditors can look up. A local class is like a scribble a teller makes on a sticky note inside one counter session — it has no official registered name and disappears when the session ends. An anonymous class is like an unnamed temporary helper with no nameplate at all. You cannot put a scribble or a nameless helper on an official permit list, so the bank's sealing system simply refuses them.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sealing needs named, compile-time-known heirs, and local and anonymous classes have no stable name to put on the permits list, so they can never be sealed.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A sealed class or interface restricts which other classes or interfaces may extend or implement it, and the permitted subtypes must be known and nameable at compile time. A local class (declared inside a method) and an anonymous class (declared inline with `new SomeType() { ... }`) cannot be `sealed`, because sealing requires an explicit, stable set of permitted subtypes identified by name, and local or anonymous types have restricted or no names and restricted scope. The compiler therefore rejects the `sealed` modifier on local and anonymous classes.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India issuing a sealed rulebook that says "only these three named account products may extend AccountProduct: Savings, Current, and FixedDeposit." For that rule to mean anything, each permitted product must have an official, registered name that auditors can look up. A local class is like a scribble a teller makes on a sticky note inside one counter session — it has no official registered name and disappears when the session ends. An anonymous class is like an unnamed temporary helper with no nameplate at all. You cannot put a scribble or a nameless helper on an official permit list, so the bank's sealing system simply refuses them.

**One line to remember:** Sealing needs named, compile-time-known heirs, and local and anonymous classes have no stable name to put on the permits list, so they can never be sealed.

sections.s2_technical:
A sealed type uses the form `public sealed interface AccountProduct permits SavingsProduct, CurrentProduct, FixedDepositProduct { }`. The `permits` clause lists the exact subtypes allowed. The compiler needs every permitted subtype to be a top-level or nested named type that it can resolve, because it writes the permitted list into the class file as the `PermittedSubclasses` attribute. A local class exists only inside a method body and cannot be referenced from a `permits` clause outside that method, so it can never appear on a permits list. For that reason the language simply forbids `sealed` on a local class. For example `void process() { sealed class Temp {} }` does not compile.

An anonymous class has no name at all. It is created with `new Runnable() { public void run() {} }`. Since sealing is fundamentally about naming a closed set of heirs, and an anonymous class can neither be named in a `permits` clause nor be named as the thing doing the sealing, `sealed` is meaningless and disallowed on anonymous classes. For example you cannot write `AccountProduct p = new sealed AccountProduct() { };` — that is a compile error.

There is a second, deeper reason. Sealed types must have a well-defined, exhaustive relationship with their permitted subtypes so the compiler can check exhaustive `switch` and so tools can reason about the closed set. Local and anonymous classes are ephemeral and scoped; the compiler cannot guarantee a stable closed hierarchy that external code can rely on. A senior nuance: an anonymous class or a local class CAN still appear as an implementor of a sealed interface when that sealed interface is `non-sealed` somewhere, but the sealed type itself and its directly permitted subtypes must be named. Also note a lambda cannot implement a sealed interface at all, because a functional interface used by a lambda must be effectively open for the compiler to synthesize the implementation.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India wants a closed, auditable set of account products. Rajesh holds a Savings account (SAV2001) and Priya holds a Current account (CUR3001). The compliance team insists that only an approved, named list of product types may ever exist, so an auditor can enumerate every possible product. This is exactly how a sealed interface works — it names the exact permitted implementors so the set is closed and provable at compile time.

Problem 2 — A junior developer tries to invent a brand new product type on the fly inside a method, as a quick local class, to handle a one-off promotional account. The bank must reject this, because an unregistered, unnamed product breaks the audit guarantee. This is exactly why Java forbids a `sealed` local class and forbids sealing anonymous classes — there is no stable name to register.

The demo will define a sealed interface `AccountProduct` with three named permitted products, show a compiling version, and then show in comments the exact code shapes (local sealed class, anonymous sealed class, lambda implementing a sealed interface) that the compiler rejects and why. We will build a small `ProductRegistry` that lists the closed set and a `BankDemo` main that processes Rajesh's and Priya's products.

Classes and steps: `AccountProduct` (sealed interface), `SavingsProduct`, `CurrentProduct`, `FixedDepositProduct` (final permitted records), `ProductRegistry` (enumerates the closed set), and `BankDemo` (main that prints each product's monthly charge and shows rejected shapes in comments).


sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's savings product (SAV2001, balance Rs.1,000,000) and Priya's current product (CUR3001, balance Rs.250,000).

Step 1 — The compiler reads `AccountProduct` and sees the `permits` clause naming exactly three types. It writes these three names into the class file's `PermittedSubclasses` attribute. At this moment the closed set is frozen; there is no slot for an unnamed local or anonymous type.

Step 2 — `BankDemo.main` creates a `SavingsProduct` for Rajesh and a `CurrentProduct` for Priya. Both are named, final, permitted implementors, so the assignment to the `AccountProduct` reference is legal.

Step 3 — `monthlyCharge` runs an exhaustive `switch`. Because the set is closed and named, the compiler proves all cases are covered and requires no `default`. Rajesh's savings product returns Rs.0, Priya's current product returns Rs.500.

Step 4 — `ProductRegistry.permittedNames` reads the same closed set reflectively via `getPermittedSubclasses` and returns the three registered names. The local and anonymous shapes in the comments never reach this stage because they fail at compile time.

```
2026-10-26 14:55:11 [INFO] Rajesh product monthly charge: Rs.0
2026-10-26 14:55:11 [INFO] Priya product monthly charge: Rs.500
2026-10-26 14:55:11 [INFO] Closed set of permitted products: [SavingsProduct, CurrentProduct, FixedDepositProduct]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Compile time: javac reads AccountProduct.java
    │ permits SavingsProduct, CurrentProduct, FixedDepositProduct
    │ writes PermittedSubclasses attribute  →  closed set FROZEN
    ▼
  Runtime: BankDemo.main
    │ new SavingsProduct("SAV2001", 1,000,000)   ← named, permitted
    │ new CurrentProduct("CUR3001",   250,000)   ← named, permitted
    ▼
  monthlyCharge(product)  — exhaustive switch (no default)
    ├─ SavingsProduct  ───→ Rs.0
    ├─ CurrentProduct  ───→ Rs.500
    └─ FixedDeposit    ───→ Rs.0
    ▼
  ProductRegistry.permittedNames()
    │ getPermittedSubclasses() → [Savings, Current, FixedDeposit]
    ▼
  REJECTED at compile time (never run):
    sealed local class no stable name
    sealed anonymous class no name at all
    lambda implements sealed cannot synthesize impl
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A sealed class or interface restricts which types may extend or implement it, and every permitted subtype must be a named type known at compile time, because the compiler records that closed set in the class file's permitted-subclasses attribute. A local class and an anonymous class can never be sealed. A local class has a name that exists only inside one method, so it can never be referenced from a permits clause elsewhere, and an anonymous class has no name at all, so there is literally nothing to list as a permitted subtype or as the sealing type itself. On top of that, sealing exists to give a stable, provable closed hierarchy, and local and anonymous types are ephemeral and scoped, so they cannot provide that guarantee.

In my banking work at National Bank of India I used a sealed interface called AccountProduct that permitted exactly three named records: a savings product, a current product, and a fixed deposit product. That closed set matched our compliance requirement that an auditor must be able to enumerate every possible product type. Rajesh's savings account and Priya's current account both map to permitted records, and because the set is closed I can write an exhaustive switch to compute monthly charges with no default branch, which means the compiler itself catches me if I ever forget a product type.

When a junior engineer tried to introduce a quick one-off promotional product as a local sealed class inside a method, the compiler rejected it, and that rejection is actually the feature working correctly. If the language allowed sealing a local or anonymous class, the closed-set guarantee would be meaningless because those types cannot be named on a permits list. I also make sure the team knows a lambda cannot implement a sealed interface either, for the same naming and closed-set reasons.

So my short answer in an interview is that sealing requires named, compile-time-known heirs, local classes have method-scoped names and anonymous classes have no names, therefore neither can be sealed, and that restriction is exactly what preserves the audit-grade closed hierarchy I rely on in production.

keyPoints: Anonymous class: inline implementation with no name
Used for: one-time event handlers, callbacks, comparators
Can extend a class OR implement one interface (not both)
Captured variables must be effectively final
